diveTitle: What actually happens when you convert
diveSubtitle: How resolution and format choices affect your images.
dive1Title: One JPG per page — how the conversion works
dive1Desc: Every page in your PDF becomes its own separate JPG image, numbered in page order. A 10-page PDF produces 10 individual JPG files, not one combined image — you download them individually or all together as a ZIP.
dive2Title: What resolution do the output images have?
dive2Desc: Pages are rendered at a resolution high enough for on-screen viewing and most printing needs — a good middle ground between image sharpness and file size. For maximum resolution needed in large-format printing, an export from the original document editor is usually a better source.
dive3Desc: JPG doesn't support transparency at all — a fundamental limitation of the format, not something our converter chooses. If your PDF page has a transparent background element, it gets filled with white in the JPG output; use PDF to PNG instead if you need to preserve transparency.
dive4Title: Converting a scanned PDF vs. a digital PDF
dive4Desc: Both convert the same way, since the tool captures a visual snapshot of each page rather than reading text content. A scanned page becomes a JPG of the scan; a digitally created page becomes a JPG of how it renders — no OCR or text extraction happens in either case.
dive5Desc: For multi-page PDFs, you can download each JPG individually or grab all of them together as a single ZIP file, which is faster for documents with more than a handful of pages instead of downloading one at a time.
dive6Title: PDF to JPG vs. PDF to PNG — which do you need?
dive6Desc: Choose JPG for photos, scanned documents, and anything where a small file size matters more than pixel-perfect sharpness. Choose PNG when the page has text you want to stay crisp, a transparent background, or when you'll edit the image further and want to avoid compression artifacts.

faq3Question: How many pages can I convert at once?

faq4Question: Will the colors and text look the same in JPG?
faq4Answer: In the vast majority of cases, yes. Our rendering engine processes each page faithfully, preserving colors, fonts, and layouts accurately. The only exception is that JPG doesn't support transparency — any transparent areas will be filled with white.

faq6Question: Can I use the JPG files commercially?

seoSection1Title: When Should You Convert PDF to JPG?
seoSection1Para1: JPG is one of the most universally compatible image formats in the world. It opens in every browser, every image viewer, every phone, and every design tool — without needing any special software. When you need to share a page from a PDF, embed it in a presentation, upload it to a website, or use it in a document where PDFs aren't accepted, converting to JPG is the practical solution.
seoSection1Para2: Our converter gives you genuine quality control. At 300 DPI, the output is sharp enough for professional printing. At 150 DPI, file sizes stay small and manageable for email and web use. At 600 DPI, you get archival-grade detail that holds up under close inspection or large-format printing. Whatever your use case, there's a setting that fits.
seoSection2Title: JPG vs PNG — Which Should You Use?
seoSection2Para: JPG and PNG are both great image formats, but they serve different purposes. JPG is ideal when file size matters — it compresses images efficiently, making it perfect for sharing, uploading, and everyday use. PNG is better when you need lossless quality or transparency support. For most PDF-to-image use cases — presentations, social media, documents, web pages — JPG is the right choice. If you need transparent backgrounds or pixel-perfect accuracy for design work, use our PDF to PNG converter instead.
seoSection3Title: Common Uses for PDF to JPG Conversion
seoSection3Para: Professionals convert PDF reports and charts into JPGs for embedding in PowerPoint slides. Marketing teams extract product images from design PDFs for use on websites and social media. Teachers pull diagrams and illustrations from course materials for use in other formats. Lawyers and archivists save scanned documents as JPG images for records management systems. Developers extract visual assets from technical documentation. Whatever your reason, SmallPDF.us handles the conversion quickly, privately, and for free.
